### Azure lazy construction never re-reads environment variables **High Severity** Azure's `_make_client_kwargs` only checks `self.api_key` and `self.endpoint` without re-reading from the environment, unlike OpenAI and Anthropic whose `_get_client_params` methods do `self.api_key = os.getenv(...)` when the field is `None`. ### Azure `is_azure_openai_endpoint` stays stale after lazy init **High Severity** When the Azure endpoint is not available at construction time, `_normalize_azure_fields` sets `is_azure_openai_endpoint = False`. Later, `_make_client_kwargs` lazily resolves the endpoint from env vars and sets `self.endpoint`, but never recalculates `is_azure_openai_endpoint`. This flag is used in `_prepare_completion_params` to decide whether to include the `model` parameter — Azure OpenAI endpoints embed the deployment name in the URL, so `model` must be omitted. With the flag stuck at `False`, every lazily-initialized Azure OpenAI endpoint will incorrectly send `model` in API requests, likely causing errors.

Re-reviewed after the 14 new commits (Apr 11–12). All looking solid.

**Lazy client construction** — consistent pattern across all 5 providers (`_init_clients` → `_build_sync_client`/`_build_async_client` → `_get_sync_client`/`_get_async_client`). All call sites properly routed through the lazy accessors.

**Azure env var re-read & endpoint recompute** (`ad6d7fa`, `60e8a4a`) — the most critical fixes. `_make_client_kwargs()` correctly re-reads `AZURE_API_KEY`/`AZURE_ENDPOINT` when fields are still falsy, and recomputes `is_azure_openai_endpoint` so the model-in-body routing stays correct. Clean extraction of `_is_azure_openai_endpoint` static method.

**Azure `aclose` no-op** (`8312e1c`) — simple null guard prevents `_get_async_client()` from triggering lazy construction during cleanup. Good regression test.

**Anthropic httpx.Client leak** (`755b1f2`) — `include_http_client=False` from the async builder is clean and backward-compatible.

**Bedrock narrowed exceptions** (`4c3ff7d`) — `(BotoCoreError, ClientError, ValueError)` covers the credential/config failure surface. `NoCredentialsError`/`PartialCredentialsError` are `BotoCoreError` subclasses, so covered. Programming errors now propagate as intended.

**Gemini** — env var re-read + `_get_client_params` null guard + async routing through `_get_async_client` all look correct.

**validate.py** — well-structured with proper severity separation, ordered checks with early-exit, good subprocess-based import classification, and solid test coverage (430 lines, 25+ cases).

**Missing-extra classifier regex** (`1121969`) — matching real error strings now instead of the backtick-delimited test artifacts. Parametrized test is a good regression guard.

### Fallback triggers too broadly for unset streaming capability **Medium Severity** The condition `not (agent_card.capabilities and agent_card.capabilities.streaming)` falls back to polling whenever `capabilities` is `None` or `streaming` is `None`, not just when `streaming` is explicitly `False`. Since `AgentCapabilities.streaming` defaults to `None` in the A2A SDK, agents that simply don't declare streaming support (leaving `streaming` unset) now get polling instead of the previous streaming default. This is a broader behavior change than intended by the PR, which specifically targets agents that advertise `streaming=False`. Using `agent_card.capabilities.streaming is False` would match only the explicit opt-out case.
 
Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 7169d03b8098917fd09faf9c13471b1264ad9212. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).

### Multimodal support broken for non-OpenAI LLM providers **High Severity** The `isinstance` check was narrowed from `BaseLLM` to `OpenAICompletion`, which means multimodal file handling in task prompts no longer works for Anthropic, Azure, Bedrock, or Gemini providers — all of which implement `supports_multimodal()` and previously matched the `BaseLLM` check. This causes `supported_types` to stay empty for those providers, so files that were previously auto-injected into prompts will instead be listed as tool-accessible files (or ignored).
 
Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit af612b05e00a8bb37490cc52f46a32b45b6cb150. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).

body:
Two of the three changes look good, but the multimodal narrowing is a regression:

**✅ Validation unrolling** — Expanding `validate_required_fields` from a loop to explicit field checks is cleaner and gives better error messages. Good.

**✅ Crew access** — `self.agent.crew` + `not isinstance(crew, str)` is tighter than `getattr` + `hasattr`. Good.

**❌ Multimodal isinstance narrowing** — Changing `isinstance(self.agent.llm, BaseLLM)` to `isinstance(self.agent.llm, OpenAICompletion)` breaks multimodal file auto-injection for **Anthropic and Gemini** providers, which both implement `supports_multimodal()` (Claude 3+ and Gemini models). With this change, files attached to tasks using those providers would fall through to the tool-readable path instead of being auto-injected into the prompt.

The `provider`/`api` attribute access cleanup is valid since those are `BaseLLM` fields, but should keep `isinstance(self.agent.llm, BaseLLM)` as the guard. Something like:

```python
if (
    isinstance(self.agent.llm, BaseLLM)
    and self.agent.llm.supports_multimodal()
):
    provider: str = self.agent.llm.provider or self.agent.llm.model
    api: str | None = self.agent.llm.api
```

This preserves the typing improvement without breaking non-OpenAI multimodal providers.

### Wrong type check for streaming last_chunk tool extraction **Medium Severity** In the sync streaming path's "Check for tool calls in the final response" (section 7), `last_chunk` is a streaming chunk — a `ModelResponseStream` instance. However, the code checks `isinstance(last_chunk, ModelResponse)`, and since `ModelResponse` and `ModelResponseStream` are sibling classes (both inherit from `ModelResponseBase`), this check is always `False` for streaming chunks. This causes `tool_calls` to remain `None`, so the post-stream tool call extraction silently fails. The same issue applies to `isinstance(choice, Choices)` — streaming choices are `LiteLLMStreamingChoices`, not `Choices`. Elsewhere in the file (e.g., lines 732, 833, 1427), the correct `ModelResponseStream` / `LiteLLMStreamingChoices` types are used for streaming chunks.
Additional Locations (1) - [`lib/crewai/src/crewai/llm.py#L885-L887`](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI/blob/bc1ab55d6a0a5e829d2fe83573f7656d9cd148f1/lib/crewai/src/crewai/llm.py#L885-L887)

body:
### Non-streaming usage lost via incorrect model_extra access **High Severity** For non-streaming responses, `litellm.completion()` returns a `ModelResponse` instance (a subclass of `ModelResponseBase`). `ModelResponse` declares `usage` as a regular Pydantic field — not an extra. In Pydantic, declared fields are never present in `model_extra`; that dict only holds undeclared keys when `extra="allow"` is set. So `response.model_extra.get("usage")` will always return `None` for `ModelResponse` objects, silently breaking all token usage tracking and callback reporting for non-streaming calls. The old code using `getattr(response, "usage", None)` worked correctly.
Additional Locations (2) - [`lib/crewai/src/crewai/llm.py#L1152-L1157`](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI/blob/76191ab225bcb3e72caf6c1189cf95d1b0f2880a/lib/crewai/src/crewai/llm.py#L1152-L1157) - [`lib/crewai/src/crewai/llm.py#L1289-L1293`](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI/blob/76191ab225bcb3e72caf6c1189cf95d1b0f2880a/lib/crewai/src/crewai/llm.py#L1289-L1293)

### `sys.exit` in helpers bypasses resume hint display **High Severity** Several functions wrapped by the new try/except blocks — `_create_tag_and_release`, `_trigger_pypi_publish`, and `_poll_pr_until_merged` — handle errors internally by calling `sys.exit(1)`. This raises `SystemExit`, a subclass of `BaseException`, which is **not** caught by `except (subprocess.CalledProcessError, Exception)`. As a result, when these critical operations fail, the program exits immediately and no resume hint is ever displayed. This silently defeats the core purpose of the PR for the most important failure scenarios (tag creation, release publishing, PR merge polling).
Additional Locations (1) - [`lib/devtools/src/crewai_devtools/cli.py#L2003-L2018`](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI/blob/9de0b2d719536beb9e0ac4e07e8ba0b586e8a318/lib/devtools/src/crewai_devtools/cli.py#L2003-L2018)

### Project ID header never injected into API client **High Severity** The `_build_client` method injects the critical `X-Watsonx-Project-Id` header, but it overrides a method that doesn't exist in the parent `OpenAICompletion` class. The parent creates `self.client` and `self.async_client` directly in its `__init__` without calling any `_build_client` hook. As a result, the project ID header is never applied to the actual HTTP clients, and all watsonx.ai API requests will lack the required project context. The `WatsonxCompletion.__init__` needs to pass `default_headers` containing the project ID to `super().__init__()`.

### Redundant GitHub API calls in template selection flow **Medium Severity** When `list_templates` calls `add_template`, it passes only the stripped `template_name`. ### `object.__setattr__` bypasses `threading.local` thread isolation **Medium Severity** `object.__setattr__(_resolving_refs_local, "refs", refs)` bypasses `threading.local`'s custom `__setattr__`, which is responsible for acquiring the internal lock and routing the write to the correct per-thread dictionary. This defeats the stated purpose of using `threading.local` and can cause false cycle detection or missed cycles when schemas are resolved concurrently. The fix is to use normal attribute assignment: `_resolving_refs_local.refs = refs`.

For a schema where definition A references B and B references A, each expansion creates fresh objects, recursing infinitely despite the guard. The `seen` set only protects against in-memory Python object cycles, which don't arise in JSON-parsed data passed to this function's callers (`_common_strict_pipeline`, `generate_model_description`).

### Redundant `RecursionError` in exception handler tuple **Low Severity** `RecursionError` is a subclass of `RuntimeError`, which is a subclass of `Exception`. Writing `except (RecursionError, Exception)` is equivalent to just `except Exception`. Listing `RecursionError` explicitly alongside `Exception` is misleading — it implies `RecursionError` wouldn't be caught by `Exception` alone, which could confuse future maintainers about Python's exception hierarchy.

### Accumulated stream IDs cause cross-contamination in same-context usage **Medium Severity** `_current_stream_ids` is append-only — IDs are added in `create_streaming_state` but never removed. When two streaming kickoffs are created sequentially from the same context (e.g. `out1 = crew1.kickoff(); out2 = crew2.kickoff()`), both stream IDs accumulate in the caller's context. Because `create_chunk_generator` lazily copies the context at iteration time (not at creation time), both worker threads inherit both IDs. Events from either worker then pass the `stream_id not in _current_stream_ids.get()` check for both handlers, defeating the isolation that this PR intends to provide. The test avoids this by using pre-isolated `contextvars.copy_context()` contexts but the real production call sites share a single calling context.

### Restored models get stricter config than originals **Medium Severity** `_deserialize_model_class` calls `create_model_from_schema(v)` without passing a `__config__` argument. body:
Solid fix for the `ModelMetaclass` serialization error during checkpoint writes.

**Approach:**
- `PlainSerializer` → `model_json_schema()` for JSON output (`when_used='json'` keeps in-memory usage unchanged)
- `BeforeValidator` → `create_model_from_schema()` to reconstruct models from stored schemas on restore
- Leverages the existing `pydantic_schema_utils` infrastructure already battle-tested for A2A

**Fields covered:** `output_json`, `output_pydantic`, `response_model`, `converter_cls`

**One note on `converter_cls`:** The deserializer correctly drops to `None` for dict values since `Converter` has methods/behavior that can't be reconstructed from a JSON schema alone. This means a restored checkpoint won't have a custom converter — but that's the right tradeoff since the alternative is a broken deserialization. If this ever matters, it can be addressed separately.

Closes #5544 part 2. LGTM ✅

body:
Solid work — well-structured event family with good recursion prevention. A few observations:

**Design ✅**
- Clean event hierarchy: three base events (write, fork, restore) + pruned as one-shot. Literal type discriminators are good for downstream consumers.
- Recursion prevention is belt-and-suspenders: emitting with `cfg`/`self` as source (so `_find_checkpoint` returns None) AND the explicit `isinstance` early-return in `_on_any_event`. Good.
- Provider interface change (`prune → int`) is well-scoped and documented.

**Minor notes (non-blocking):**
- In `_do_checkpoint`, `duration_ms` is captured before pruning but `CheckpointCompletedEvent` emits after pruning — so the completed event's timing is accurate for the write, but consumers might expect it to be the total latency. Might be worth a docstring note.
- The `fork()` try/except around `self._branch = new_branch` is effectively dead code (string assignment can't fail), but harmless as future-proofing if fork logic grows.
- The `**context` splat in `_do_checkpoint` assumes the incoming event has `task_id`/`task_name`/`agent_id`/`agent_role` — should be fine for crew/task lifecycle events that trigger checkpoints, but could `AttributeError` if a custom event without those fields somehow triggers a checkpoint. Low risk given `_should_checkpoint` filtering.

👍

body:
### Prune failure prevents CheckpointCompletedEvent from being emitted **Medium Severity** In `_do_checkpoint`, the `cfg.provider.prune()` call (line 178) sits between the successful checkpoint write and the `CheckpointCompletedEvent` emission (line 195). If `prune()` raises an exception, the `CheckpointCompletedEvent` is never emitted even though the checkpoint was already written successfully and lineage was updated via `_chain_lineage`. Observability listeners pairing started/completed events will see `CheckpointStartedEvent` with no terminal event, creating an inconsistent lifecycle.
 
Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 025ca4ba9d0baeb7a33a847ddc3be5e3efa63b55. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).

body:
### Completed event `parent_id` always equals `checkpoint_id` after lineage mutation **Medium Severity** `_chain_lineage` sets `self._parent_id = self._checkpoint_id` (i.e., the just-written checkpoint's ID) *before* `CheckpointCompletedEvent` is emitted. All CI green. Clean fix for a real serialization crash.

**What's good:**
- Root cause is correct: `model_dump(mode="json")` can't handle `ModelMetaclass` — the `PlainSerializer` approach is the right pattern.
- Serialization strategy is sensible: class refs → JSON schema under a sentinel marker, instances → `model_dump(mode="json")`, dicts passthrough, unknown `type` values → `None`.
- `BeforeValidator` for deserialization with `create_model_from_schema` handles the round-trip. Good that the test verifies the rehydrated model has the expected fields.
- Test coverage is solid — class ref, instance, dict, and round-trip cases all covered.

**A few observations (non-blocking):**

1. **Lossy round-trip for class refs**: Serializing a class as its JSON schema and rehydrating via `create_model_from_schema` produces a *new* dynamically-generated class, not the original `MyState`. This means `isinstance(state, MyState)` would fail after restore. That's probably fine for checkpoint use (you just need the shape), but worth noting in the docstring.

2. **`type[dict]` in the union**: The type annotation includes `type[dict]` but `_serialize_initial_state` would hit the `isinstance(value, type)` branch and return `None` for it (since `dict` isn't a `BaseModel` subclass). Technically correct behavior (can't serialize a bare `dict` class), but the annotation suggests it's a supported input that would survive serialization.

3. **Sentinel key in user data**: If someone's actual state dict happens to contain `__crewai_pydantic_class_schema__` as a key, the deserializer would misinterpret it. Extremely unlikely but the double-underscore prefix helps.

LGTM 👍

body:
This is a well-thought-out addition. The checkpoint resume timeline gap is a real UX problem and replaying stored events is the right fix. CI still running but the approach is sound.

**Design**
- `replay()` as a distinct method from `emit()` is the right call — keeping the "no _prepare_event" semantics explicit rather than adding a flag to `emit()`.
- ContextVar-based `is_replaying()` is clean and thread-safe. The token-on-calling-thread + dedicated `_acall_handlers_replaying`/`_emit_with_dependencies_replaying` wrappers handle cross-thread propagation correctly.
- Checkpoint listener opt-out is minimal — just the `is_replaying()` early-return at the top of `_on_any_event`. Good placement.
- Sorting replayed events by `emission_sequence` preserves causal ordering.

**One potential issue (non-blocking but worth checking):**
In `replay()`, when both `sync_handlers` and `async_handlers` exist, the sync future is submitted via `self._sync_executor.submit()` but `_track_future()` is only called on the async future (the `if not async_handlers: return` branch is skipped). The sync future becomes fire-and-forget — if a sync handler raises, the exception is silently swallowed. For MethodExecution events this is likely fine (most handlers are side-effect-free timeline listeners), but it could mask issues.

**Tests** — solid coverage: field preservation, flag toggling, checkpoint opt-out, and E2E resume scenario.

LGTM

### Replay emits duplicate events for non-completed methods **Medium Severity** `_replay_recorded_events` replays every `MethodExecution*` event in the record without filtering by `self._completed_methods`. When the event record contains events for methods that are *not* in the completed set (e.g., a method that started but didn't finish before the checkpoint, or a shared runtime state from a prior full run), those events get replayed *and* the method re-executes normally — producing duplicate `MethodExecutionStartedEvent`/`FinishedEvent` entries in the trace timeline. The node filter needs an additional check like `n.event.method_name in self._completed_methods` to only replay events belonging to methods that will be skipped on resume.
 
Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 3a359a5fa60c57db38f66b7315428f31c1774396. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).

body:
Re-reviewed after two new commits (23db2669 + ec985359). Good improvements:

**Commit 2 (23db2669) — addresses my sync future note:**
- `_track_future(sync_future)` is now called even when async handlers exist — sync futures are no longer fire-and-forget. 👍
- Replay now filters to `self._completed_methods` — prevents replaying events for methods that are about to re-execute.
- E2E test assertions tightened from `in` to `count == 1`.

**Commit 3 (ec985359) — fork/restore scope cleanup:**
- `restore_event_scope(())` + `reset_last_event_id()` in `_restore_from_checkpoint` — clears stale event context so resumed methods get fresh parent chains. Good.
- Fork now generates a new flow state `id` via `uuid4()` — ensures forked flows have distinct identities. Clean.

**CI is red** — `test_resume_dispatches_completed_method_events` fails:
```
assert 4 == 1
  where 4 = ["step_a", "step_a", "step_a", "step_a", "step_b", "step_b", "step_b", "step_b", "step_c"].count("step_a")
```

`step_a` fires 4 times instead of 1. Likely cause: the `scoped_handlers()` context manager is not isolating properly — handlers from the first `flow1.kickoff()` are still active when `flow2.kickoff()` runs, AND the replay adds another round. Since `flow1.kickoff()` runs before the `scoped_handlers()` block, its events are captured by the handlers registered inside the block if the bus is shared. The test needs either:
1. Move `flow1.kickoff()` outside any handler scope (which it already is — so the issue is likely that `flow2.kickoff()` re-executes step_a+step_b via normal flow execution AND replays them)
2. The completed_methods filter should prevent step_a/step_b from re-executing via normal flow, but `step_c` listener triggers from step_b, and if replay emits MethodExecutionFinished for step_b, the flow listener graph might fire step_c... which then also emits step_c started/finished naturally.

The 4x count suggests events are being captured from: (a) replay of step_a started, (b) normal re-execution of step_a (if _completed_methods is not skipping start methods), (c) possibly duplicate handler registration. Worth debugging.

### Direct node access bypasses EventRecord's read lock **Low Severity** `_replay_recorded_events` accesses `record.nodes.values()` directly, bypassing the `EventRecord`'s `RWLock` that all other accessors (`add`, `get`, `descendants`, `roots`, `__len__`, `__contains__`) use. If any concurrent thread is writing to the record via `add()` (which acquires a write lock), iterating over `nodes` without the read lock is a data race. While CPython's GIL makes this unlikely to crash in practice, it violates the locking contract established by `EventRecord`.

body:
## Consolidated PR Review — Valkey Storage Implementation

**Reviewers:** GLIDE API validation, Python code quality / DRY, Security (OWASP methodology)
**19 files, +9276 / -904 lines, ~5300 lines of tests**

See inline comments for specific findings at the relevant lines.

- 🔴 **5 must-fix:** FT.SEARCH query injection via `=>` token, wrong import paths (`ImportError`), key construction injection, TLS cert params are silent no-ops, credentials set post-construction
- 🟡 **7 suggestions:** Use `ft.list()` not `ft.info()` for index check, N+1 query patterns, duplicated client init, duplicated category parsing (4×), duplicated bytes decoding (5×), dead `_retry_operation`, pagination fetches all records first
- 🟢 **7 low items:** Positional GLIDE API args, scan cursor type, f-strings in logging, deprecated `datetime.utcnow()`, TOCTOU in index creation, no batching for bulk saves, `_run_async` returns `Any`

### ✅ Security Assessment
- 1 HIGH: FT.SEARCH `=>` injection via LLM-inferred scope/category values
- 2 MEDIUM: Key construction injection, TLS cert silent no-ops

### ✅ GLIDE API
- Correct `ft.create(client, ...)` / `ft.search(client, ...)` module-level pattern ✅
- Correct KNN query syntax with filter expressions ✅
- Correct binary embedding handling with numpy float32 ✅
- Import paths need fixing (internal `glide.async_commands` vs stable `glide_shared`) ❌

### ✅ What's Done Well
- Comprehensive 5300-line test suite covering CRUD, search, scopes, errors, cache
- Correct cosine distance→similarity conversion
- Lazy client init, connection timeouts, retry logic design
- Thread-safe sync/async bridge with persistent background event loop
- Optional peer dependency — no impact on non-Valkey users
- Proper integration into unified memory, encoding flow, A2A cache
- Good documentation with docstrings and forward-compat notes
author: Jonathan-Improving

body:
🔴 **[SECURITY HIGH] FT.SEARCH query injection via `=>` token**

The escape method does not block the `=>` two-character sequence, which is the KNN clause delimiter in Valkey Search. Since scope and category values can be LLM-inferred from agent content (attacker-influenced), a crafted scope value containing `=>` could inject an arbitrary KNN clause, bypassing scope isolation and potentially exfiltrating cross-tenant memories.

**Fix:** Add `=>` to the escape list, or escape `>` individually (which is already partially covered but the two-char sequence `=>` has special meaning beyond the individual chars).
author: Jonathan-Improving

body:
🔴 **Wrong import paths — will cause `ImportError`**

These import paths use `glide.async_commands.server_modules.ft_options.*` but the correct paths are `glide_shared.commands.server_modules.ft_options.*` (or use top-level `glide` exports which re-export these types).

The `glide.async_commands` path is an internal implementation detail that may not be stable across versions.
author: Jonathan-Improving

body:
🔴 **[SECURITY MEDIUM] Key construction injection via unsanitized inputs**

These key helpers use `:` as a delimiter with unsanitized inputs. Since scope, category, and metadata values can be LLM-inferred from agent content, values containing `:` cause key collisions between index structures, enabling cross-scope data leakage.

For example, `scope="/agent"` + `category="test:scope:/other"` could create a key `category:test:scope:/other` that collides with the scope index namespace.

**Fix:** Validate inputs against an allowlist regex, or use a collision-resistant encoding (e.g., base64 or URL-encoding the dynamic parts).
author: Jonathan-Improving

body:
🔴 **TLS certificate parameters are silent no-ops — false sense of security**

`tls_ca_cert_path`, `tls_client_cert_path`, and `tls_client_key_path` are accepted and stored but never wired into the GLIDE client configuration. A user who provides custom certificates gets no error and no actual certificate verification beyond system defaults.

**Fix:** Either wire these into `AdvancedGlideClientConfiguration` with `TlsAdvancedConfiguration(root_pem_cacerts=...)`, or raise `NotImplementedError` with a clear message explaining the GLIDE Python binding limitation, rather than silently accepting and ignoring them.
author: Jonathan-Improving

body:
🔴 **`config.credentials` set post-construction**

`GlideClientConfiguration` should receive credentials in the constructor, not via attribute assignment after construction. The current approach may not work correctly depending on the GLIDE version, as the config object may not support post-init mutation.

```python
# Fix:
config = GlideClientConfiguration(
    addresses=[NodeAddress(host, port)],
    database_id=db,
    credentials=ServerCredentials(password=self._password) if self._password else None,
)
```
author: Jonathan-Improving

body:
🟡 **Use `ft.list()` instead of `ft.info()` for index existence check**

`ft.info()` raises `RequestError` on missing indices, which you catch with a bare `except Exception`. `ft.list()` returns a list of index names without raising, making the check cleaner and avoiding the exception-as-control-flow pattern.

```python
# Fix:
existing = await ft.list(client)
names = {i.decode() if isinstance(i, bytes) else str(i) for i in (existing or [])}
if "memory_index" in names:
    self._index_created = True
    return
```
author: Jonathan-Improving

body:
🟡 **`_retry_operation` is defined but never called — dead code**

This method implements retry with exponential backoff but is never invoked by any of the storage operations (`asave`, `_aupdate`, `adelete`, `_vector_search`, etc.). Either wire it into the operations that need retry, or remove it.
author: Jonathan-Improving

body: **Correction:** Downgrading from 🔴 SECURITY MEDIUM to 🟢 informational. After cross-referencing with the Valkey GLIDE skill documentation, `:` is the standard key delimiter used throughout all GLIDE examples and patterns. This is a data integrity concern (crafted values could cause key collisions) but not a security vulnerability in the Valkey sense. The `=>` injection (finding #1) remains the real security issue in this PR.
author: Jonathan-Improving

body: **Correction:** Downgrading from 🔴 to 🟡 suggestion. The GLIDE skill documentation shows the constructor pattern but does not indicate that post-construction assignment fails. This is a style preference for consistency with documented patterns, not a confirmed functional bug. The suggested constructor approach is still recommended but the current code likely works.

### Fork with pinned id incorrectly skips execution state reset **Low Severity** The `is_restoring` check doesn't account for `restore_from_state_id`. When both `inputs["id"]` and `restore_from_state_id` are provided with persistence enabled, `is_restoring` evaluates to `True`, which prevents clearing `_completed_methods`, `_method_outputs`, and other execution state. A fork is intended to be a fresh execution with hydrated data state, but this path treats it as a resume. On a reused `Flow` instance, leftover `_completed_methods` from a prior run would cause `_is_execution_resuming` to be set to `True`, incorrectly skipping already-completed methods instead of re-executing them.

### copy.copy fails on LiteLLM-backed LLM instances **High Severity** `copy.copy(self.llm)` will raise `TypeError` for LiteLLM-backed `LLM` instances. The `LLM` class defines `__new__(cls, model: str, ...)` with `model` as a required positional argument. Pydantic's `BaseModel.__copy__` internally calls `cls.__new__(cls)` without additional arguments, which fails when `type(self.llm)` is `LLM` (the LiteLLM fallback path). Native provider subclasses (e.g., `OpenAICompletion`) don't override `__new__` so they work fine — and the tests only use `LLM(model="gpt-4")` which creates a native instance, masking this bug. Using `self.llm.model_copy()` instead of `copy.copy(self.llm)` would avoid the issue.

body:
**Security Issues**
- Deserialization of Untrusted Data (Pickle) in cache backend
The Aiocache-backed paths in UploadCache use PickleSerializer when connecting to Redis. Retrieving cached values unpickles arbitrary data from a network-accessible cache. If an attacker can write or influence Redis/aiocache contents (e.g., via a misconfigured or compromised Redis instance), this can lead to remote code execution in the application process on cache get. The new Valkey backend correctly uses JSON, but the Aiocache (Redis/memory) path continues to use pickle.

Recommendations
- Avoid pickle for data stored in Redis/remote caches. Use a safe, deterministic format (JSON) and explicitly serialize/deserialize objects (e.g., CachedUpload.to_dict()/from_dict()) for the Aiocache backend as done for ValkeyCacheBackend.
- If JSON cannot be used immediately, restrict aiocache to in-memory only for pickle usage and never configure a networked Redis backend with PickleSerializer.
- Enforce authentication and TLS for Redis if it must be used, but prefer eliminating pickle altogether for networked caches.
author: corridor-security

body:
Using PickleSerializer with a Redis-backed aiocache unpickles arbitrary data received from a network-accessible cache. If an attacker can write to or influence the Redis instance (e.g., misconfiguration, shared cache), they can craft a malicious pickle to achieve code execution upon `get()`.

Vulnerable snippets:
```python
return AiocacheBackend(
    Cache(
        Cache.REDIS,
        serializer=PickleSerializer(),
        namespace=namespace,
        **cache_kwargs,
    )
)
```
and
```python
return AiocacheBackend(
    Cache(serializer=PickleSerializer(), namespace=namespace)
)
```

The Valkey backend correctly uses JSON serialization, but the Aiocache (Redis) path still uses pickle.

Remediation: Replace pickle with a safe format (JSON) and explicitly serialize/deserialize `CachedUpload` for the Aiocache path, mirroring `ValkeyCacheBackend`'s approach. If that refactor is non-trivial, avoid using Redis with `PickleSerializer` entirely — limit pickle to Process-local memory caches only and never over the network.

For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/b733a111-d5fe-4e2c-8059-6ab1d477042c/findings/cbe1a289-b28e-4b30-aac0-62647b16f560).

**Provide feedback**: Reply with whether this is a valid vulnerability or false positive to help improve Corridor's accuracy.
author: corridor-security

body:
Valid finding, but pre-existing — the PickleSerializer usage in the aiocache Redis path predates this PR. We didn't introduce or modify that serialization path, only refactored where the aiocache config is set up.

Our new Valkey backend uses JSON serialization exclusively (as corridor-security correctly notes). Replacing pickle in the legacy aiocache Redis path is a separate concern and will be tracked as a follow-up.

Yes. concurrent.futures.Future.result(timeout=...) is a blocking call: if the Future hasn’t completed, it waits up to the timeout, and if not completed it raises concurrent.futures.TimeoutError; during that wait the event-loop thread is blocked and cannot run other callbacks/coroutines [1][2]. 2) If Future.result(timeout=...) times out, does the running worker remain occupied? Yes. Timeout only affects the waiting caller: result(timeout=...) raises TimeoutError when the result wasn’t ready within the timeout, but it does not stop/kill the running callable in the executor; the worker thread can remain occupied until the callable cooperatively finishes. This is consistent with executor semantics: there is no API to terminate a running thread; canceling a Future prevents work that hasn’t started, but cannot abruptly stop work already running [3]. 3) Recommended pattern for offloading blocking synchronous work from async code Use asyncio’s executor offloading APIs and await them instead of blocking on.result in the loop thread: - Preferred (Python 3.9+): asyncio.to_thread for IO-bound blocking functions [4]. - Generic: await loop.run_in_executor(executor, func, *args), where the executor is a concurrent.futures.Executor (often a ThreadPoolExecutor for blocking IO) [5]. - If you need a timeout, apply it at the asyncio layer (so the event loop isn’t blocked) using asyncio.wait_for / task timeouts, rather than calling concurrent.futures.Future.result with timeout from the event-loop thread. (The docs show executor offloading; the concurrent.futures timeout is for the blocking waiter, not for event-loop-friendly cancellation) [5][1]. This keeps the event loop responsive because you await an asyncio awaitable returned by run_in_executor/to_thread instead of blocking the loop thread with Future.result. [5][4]

💡 Result:

In Python 3.10, concurrent.futures.TimeoutError and the built-in TimeoutError are distinct exception classes that are not the same and do not subclass each other[1][2][3]. The concurrent.futures module defines its own TimeoutError as a subclass of Exception (via its local Error class): class TimeoutError(Error): pass[2]. This is raised specifically when Future.result, Future.exception, as_completed, or Executor.map timeout[1]. The built-in TimeoutError is a subclass of OSError, raised for system-level timeouts like socket operations corresponding to errno.ETIMEDOUT[3]. Catching one will not catch the other unless catching the base Exception. This distinction was unified to use the built-in TimeoutError starting in Python 3.11[4][5]. Note that asyncio.TimeoutError in Python 3.10 is also separate from the built-in one[6].

gh issue create \
  --repo crewAIInc/crewAI \
  --title "feat(valkey): metadata_filter fields not indexed in memory_index FT schema" \
  --body "## Summary

The \`metadata_filter\` clauses constructed in \`ValkeyStorage._vector_search()\` reference arbitrary metadata key fields (e.g. \`@key:value\`), but the \`memory_index\` FT schema only defines the following fields:

- \`VectorField(\"embedding\")\`
- \`TagField(\"scope\")\`
- \`TagField(\"categories\")\`
- \`NumericField(\"created_at\")\`
- \`NumericField(\"importance\")\`

As a result, \`metadata_filter\` cannot actually restrict \`FT.SEARCH\` results and will either error or silently return wrong results.

**Affected file:** \`lib/crewai/src/crewai/memory/storage/valkey_storage.py\` (around lines 513–519 and 1237–1245)

## Remediation options

**Option A — Materialize metadata into the FT index:**
Add the necessary metadata fields to the \`memory_index\` schema (e.g. as \`TagField\` or \`NumericField\` depending on type) and update the schema construction accordingly. This requires defining a known set of metadata keys upfront or dynamically managing the index schema.

**Option B — Post-filter outside FT.SEARCH:**
Remove metadata clauses from the FT query in \`_vector_search()\` and instead apply \`metadata_filter\` as a post-filter over the \`FT.SEARCH\` results before returning final hits. This is simpler but may return more documents from Valkey than strictly necessary.

## Context

Raised during review of PR `#5703` (ValkeyStorage vector memory backend, part 4/4). Deferred to a follow-up PR so maintainers can decide the preferred approach, given the broader schema implications.

body:
**Security Issues**
- **SSRF bypass via DNS rebinding**
The new `_SSRFSafeAdapter` validates a hostname with `socket.getaddrinfo()`, then calls `super().send()`, where urllib3 performs a separate DNS resolution for the actual socket connection. An attacker controlling DNS for a requested or redirected hostname can return a public IP for the validation lookup and a private or metadata IP for the connection lookup, bypassing the SSRF blocklist and reaching internal services through `safe_get()` callers such as scraping and RAG loaders.

**Recommendation**
- Pin the validated IP to the actual connection, or use a custom requests/urllib3 adapter that enforces the private/reserved IP check at connect time so the socket is opened only to an address that was already vetted.
author: corridor-security

body:
The adapter validates the hostname with `socket.getaddrinfo()`, but then `super().send()` lets urllib3 resolve the hostname again for the actual socket connection:

```python
addrinfos = socket.getaddrinfo(parsed.hostname, port)
...
return super().send(request, **kwargs)
```

Because these are separate DNS lookups, an attacker who controls DNS for the requested or redirected hostname can use DNS rebinding: return a public IP during validation, then return `169.254.169.254`, `127.0.0.1`, or another private/internal IP during the connection lookup. That bypasses the SSRF blocklist and allows `safe_get()` callers to reach internal or cloud metadata services.

**Remediation**: Ensure the checked IP is the IP used for the TCP connection. For example, implement a custom adapter/resolver that connects to the already-validated address while preserving the original `Host` header and TLS SNI, or otherwise enforce the private/reserved IP blocklist inside the actual connection creation path.

For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/b733a111-d5fe-4e2c-8059-6ab1d477042c/findings/0b306941-69f3-48fc-8d56-287c92a6d454).

body:
**Security Issues**
- **Broken Scope Isolation via Prefix-Matching**
The updated LanceDB filters now escape SQL metacharacters, but they still append `%` directly to caller-supplied scope prefixes. A caller scoped to `/alpha` will also match `/alpha2`, `/alphabet`, or `/alpha-private` in `search`, `_scan_rows`-based readers, and `delete`, allowing cross-scope reads or deletes without needing SQL injection. Enforce a path boundary with an exact scope match or a child-scope match such as `scope = prefix OR scope LIKE prefix + '/%'`.
author: corridor-security

body:
The escaped `LIKE` still treats the caller-provided scope as an unbounded string prefix:

```python
like_val = self._escape_like(prefix) + "%"
query = query.where(f"scope LIKE '{like_val}' ESCAPE '\\'")
```

If a caller is authorized only for `scope_prefix="/alpha"`, this also matches `/alpha2`, `/alphabet`, or `/alpha-private`, allowing reads from sibling scopes. The same `prefix + "%"` pattern is also used in `delete()` and `_scan_rows()`, so the issue can affect deletion, listing, counting, and category enumeration as well.

**Remediation**: enforce a scope path boundary by matching either the exact scope or descendants separated by `/`, e.g. `scope = '<prefix>' OR scope LIKE '<prefix>/%' ESCAPE '\\'`. Do not treat arbitrary string prefixes as scope containment.

For more details, see the [finding in Corridor](https://app.corridor.dev/projects/b733a111-d5fe-4e2c-8059-6ab1d477042c/findings/e0d0d26a-b497-477d-bca0-c8ae0b187962).

_⚠️ Potential issue_ | _🟠 Major_ | _⚡ Quick win_

<details>
<summary>🧩 Analysis chain</summary>

🌐 Web query:

`opensandbox python SDK WriteEntry mode parameter documentation`

💡 Result:

In the OpenSandbox Python SDK, WriteEntry.mode is the Unix file permission bits (octal integer). It’s passed as an integer like 644 or 755 when creating a WriteEntry for sandbox.files.write_files. [1][2] Documented usage (examples): - mode=644 creates a normal data file with rw-r--r-- permissions. [1] - mode=755 creates an executable script with rwxr-xr-x permissions. [1] - Common recommended values include 600 (rw-------) for sensitive files. [1] Permission meanings (octal): - 755 => rwxr-xr-x (owner read/write/execute; group/others read/execute) [3] - 644 => rw-r--r-- (owner read/write; group/others read only) [3] - 600 => rw------- (only owner read/write) [3] Therefore, WriteEntry.mode expects a numeric octal Unix mode/permission value (e.g., 644, 755, 600), and it controls the file’s permission bits inside the sandbox. [1][3]

Citations:

- 1: https://mintlify.com/alibaba/OpenSandbox/examples/file-operations
- 2: https://github.com/alibaba/OpenSandbox/blob/main/sdks/sandbox/python/README.md
- 3: https://www.mintlify.com/alibaba/OpenSandbox/api/execution/filesystem

---



</details>

**Fix Unix file mode to use octal notation.**

`mode: int = 755` is the decimal value 755, not octal. Unix file permissions should be specified in octal: `0o755` (octal) = 493 (decimal) = rwxr-xr-x permissions. The SDK interprets `mode` as octal Unix permission bits; passing 755 decimal would set permissions to `0o1363` instead of `0o755`, resulting in incorrect file permissions.
